title: Gerunds and Infinitives

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In English, when two verbs appear together, the second verb takes a specific form. Some verbs are followed by the <gerund> (-ing), others by the <infinitive> (to + verb), and some accept both.

Examples:
• I enjoy <reading> books. (gerund)
• I want <to read> a book. (infinitive)

There's no simple rule to predict the pattern — but useful groups make it easier.

sections.title: Verbs Followed by Gerund (-ing)
sections.content:
These common verbs are always followed by the <gerund> (-ing form):

<Enjoy>: I enjoy cooking. | <Avoid>: She avoids eating late.
<Mind>: Do you mind waiting? | <Suggest>: He suggested going out.
<Finish>: We finished cleaning. | <Consider>: I'm considering changing jobs.
<Keep>: She keeps forgetting her keys. | <Deny>: He denied stealing it.

Helpful trick: many of these verbs describe reactions to actions or ongoing situations.

sections.title: Verbs Followed by Infinitive (to + verb)
sections.content:
These common verbs are always followed by the <infinitive> (to + verb):

<Want>: I want to travel. | <Decide>: She decided to study medicine.
<Hope>: We hope to see you soon. | <Plan>: They plan to move.
<Agree>: He agreed to help. | <Refuse>: She refused to answer.
<Offer>: He offered to carry my bags. | <Afford>: We can't afford to buy it.

Helpful pattern: these verbs express intentions, desires, or future-oriented actions.

sections.title: Verbs That Accept Both Forms
sections.content:
Some verbs can be followed by either form with little change in meaning:

<Like>: I like swimming. / I like to swim.
<Love>: She loves dancing. / She loves to dance.
<Hate>: He hates waiting. / He hates to wait.
<Start>: It started raining. / It started to rain.
<Begin>: She began crying. / She began to cry.
<Prefer>: I prefer walking. / I prefer to walk.

With these verbs, both forms are correct. The gerund sounds slightly more informal.

sections.title: Prepositions + Gerund
sections.content:
After prepositions, always use the <gerund>, never the infinitive:

<Interested in>: She's interested in learning French.
<Good at>: He's good at solving problems.
<Tired of>: I'm tired of waiting.
<Before>: Before leaving, check your bags.
<After>: After finishing work, I went home.
<Without>: He left without saying goodbye.
<Look forward to>: I look forward to meeting you.

Note: <look forward to> uses the gerund because <to> here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

sections.title: Gerunds and Infinitives in Context
sections.content:
Example 1: JOB INTERVIEW - <Why do you want to work here? — I enjoy working with people and I decided to apply because I hope to grow professionally.>

Example 2: MAKING PLANS - <A: I suggest going to the beach this weekend.
B: I'd prefer to stay home. I don't mind relaxing here.>

Example 3: DAILY LIFE - <I finished eating and started to get ready. I avoid driving in rush hour, so I plan to take the bus.>

sections.title: Summary
sections.content:
Key points to remember:

• Verbs like enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, finish → <gerund> (-ing).
• Verbs like want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse → <infinitive> (to + verb).
• Verbs like like, love, hate, start, prefer → both forms work.
• After prepositions (interested in, good at, look forward to) → always <gerund>.
• <No universal rule> — learn patterns through practice and exposure.

learningObjectives: Identify verbs followed by gerund (-ing form)
Identify verbs followed by infinitive (to + verb)
Recognize verbs that accept both forms
Apply gerund and infinitive patterns in context

keyVocabulary.definition: The -ing form of a verb used as a noun (e.g., swimming, reading)
The base form of a verb with 'to' (e.g., to swim, to read)
The grammatical structure that follows a verb
